E062-01.notes: Two independent clauses ('the pack ice ... closed around the ship' / 'the crew could do nothing but wait'). A is a comma splice; B is a fused sentence; D puts an unneeded comma after the coordinating conjunction 'and'. C joins them correctly with comma + FANBOYS.

E062-02.notes: Simple past needed ('in November 1915 Endurance sank'). A 'sunk' is the past participle used without a helper; B 'had sank' pairs a helper with the simple-past form (should be 'had sunk') and the past perfect isn't needed anyway; C 'sinked' is not a word.

E062-03.notes: 'a barren, uninhabited place' is an appositive renaming Elephant Island, set off correctly by a comma. B: a semicolon followed by a noun-phrase fragment; C: 'which a barren, uninhabited place' has no verb; D: no comma, so the appositive runs into the noun.

E062-04.notes: 'South Georgia, where a whaling station operated' is a place clause. A: read literally, 'which a whaling station operated' makes South Georgia the object of 'operated', meaning the station ran the island, which is illogical. C 'when' refers to time, not place. D 'that' cannot follow a comma to start a nonrestrictive clause, and it has the same object problem as A. Facts check out: South Georgia had whaling stations (e.g., Stromness).

E062-05.notes: Redundancy. 'hiked' says it all. A 'hiked and walked', B 'hiked on foot by walking' and D 'walked on foot' are all redundant. Facts (Shackleton, Worsley and Crean crossing South Georgia) are accurate.

E062-06.notes: Redundancy. B, C and D each pair two words meaning 'finally' ('finally, at last'; 'at last, finally'; 'in the end, finally'). The single word 'finally' is concise and correct. Facts (fourth rescue attempt, August 1916, 22 men) are accurate.

E062-07.notes: The subject is the singular 'one' ('Not one member of the crew'), so the verb is 'was lost'. A 'were' agrees with the plural noun in the prepositional phrase ('crew'), not the subject; C 'have been' is plural and in the wrong tense for a narrative in the simple past; D 'being lost' leaves the sentence without a main verb.

E062-08.notes: 'remarkably well preserved' is a modifying phrase describing the wreck, and it takes a comma after the main clause. A: a semicolon followed by a fragment; B: with no comma, the phrase reads as if it modified 'Sea'; C: a colon after a complete clause is borderline at best, and the ACT would not treat it as the best way to attach a simple descriptive modifier. The fact checks out: in 2022 the wreck was found at about 3,008 m (about 9,870 ft).

E062-09.notes: The essay is a survival/rescue narrative. Mentioning that the wreck was found in 2022 doesn't make it a description of a scientific discovery made during an expedition, so B fails. A is false (the essay never explains how pack ice forms), and D is false (both Antarctica and the Weddell Sea are named).

flags.note: Read strictly, D 'continuously at a constant rate' is not fully redundant: 'continuously' means without interruption, and 'at a constant rate' means steady flow. Still, it is wordier than C and overlaps in meaning, so C is clearly best by the ACT's conciseness rule. Minor only.

E062-10.notes: Redundancy. 'steadily' alone carries the meaning. A stacks three synonyms ('steadily and continuously at a constant rate'); B 'steadily and at a steady pace' repeats itself; D is wordy and overlapping. The item uses a different passage (CLD-P-ACT-E-000061, Elijah McCoy). Its facts (1872 lubricator patent, more than fifty patents) are accurate.
